system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 10 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2170-05-09 00:30:00 to 2170-05-18 15:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a 58-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia s/p double cord transplant, chronic GVHD, and COP, was admitted with fever, hypotension, cough, and weakness. He was found to have left lower lobe pneumonia on chest X-ray and was treated with IV vancomycin and ceftazidime in the ICU before transitioning to oral levofloxacin. Hypotension was managed with IV fluids and stress-dose hydrocortisone, later switched back to home prednisone. Acute kidney injury, likely pre-renal, resolved with rehydration. He developed antibiotic-associated diarrhea on hospital day 5, treated empirically with metronidazole despite negative C. diff toxin tests; symptoms improved. He remained afebrile, tolerated oral intake, and was discharged home on day 7 with instructions to complete antibiotic courses and follow up with oncology. C. diff PCR remained pending at discharge.
problems: Acute myeloid leukemia, without mention of having achieved remission
Other dependence on machines, supplemental oxygen

Brief Hospital Course:
___ year old gentleman with Hx of AML, s/p cord transplant in 
___ with prior chronic GVHD on MMF and prednisone, admitted 
with symptoms of nausea, vomiting and diarrhea and eventually 
found to have norovirus infection.  He was also found to have 
transaminitis and acute renal failure on admission. Volume 
depletion and renal failure resolved, and GI symptoms gradually 
improved as well.  Transaminitis did not resolve and will be 
followed closely as an outpatient. 
.
# N/V/D:  Patient had an ongoing diarrhea and nause for several 
days. He underwent a flexible sigmoidoscopy - biopsies did not 
suggest GVH.  In the meanwhile the norovirus antigen returned 
positive.  While hospitalized, he was started on aggressive IV 
hydration.  His diet was advanced as tolerated.  At the time of 
his discharge he had no vomiting or diarrhea for > 24 hours.  He 
was discharged with a few tablets of compazine and lomotil in 
case he gets the symptoms back with instruction to call his 
provider if these recur.  
.
# Acute on chronic renal failure:  The patient was found to have 
creat of 3.0 on admission; baseline 1.8-2.0.  FeNa was <1 and 
acute renal failure thought to be in the setting of volume 
depletion secondary to multiple episodes of diarrhea and 
decreased PO intake.  The patient was also initially found to be 
orthostatic.  He was given aggressive IV hydration and the 
patient's creatinine soon trended down back to his baseline.  
All medications were renally dosed and nephrotoxic agents were 
avoided.  Upon discharge, the patient's creatinine had returned 
back to his baseline.  
.
# Transaminitis:  Patient was found to have an elevation of his 
AST and ALT.  Hepatitits studies were negative.  The 
differential included direct norovirus infections vs. GVHD 
(possibly triggered by his Norovirus infection).  The liver team 
was consulted.  The patient refused a liver biopsy during this 
admission, however he is willing to have the liver biopsy if his 
liver enzymes do not improve over time. Patient will have three 
times weekly LFT and will have a follow up with his oncologist 
and liver clinic for close follow up.  Allopurinol was stopped 
as it is a non-essential medication.
.
#  AML:  The patient is s/p cord transplant; while in patient 
his Bactrim ppx was held given his transaminitis, as above.
.
#  Chronic GVHD:  The patient has a history of GVH; in the past, 
it mostly presented with arthalgias and joint pain.  He has been 
maintained on prednisone 3mg daily, and MMF 250 mg TID. No 
changes were made to these medications.

# HTN:  The patient was continued on his home carvedilol.  
.
==========================

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you while you were hospitalized 
at ___.  You were admitted to the hospital because you were 
having many days of diarrhea and you were found to have kidney 
dysfunction.  We think that your kidneys were not working well 
because you were very dehydrated.  We gave you fluids through 
your veins and your renal function improved.

We sent your stool to the lab and found that it was positive for 
Norovirus.  We also did a flexible sigmoidoscopy that showed 
diverticulosis. Biopsies were taken and were not concerning for 
graft versus host disease. 

During your stay, your liver enzymes were elevated. We think 
this might be secondary to the Norovirus infection. However, 
graft versus host disease of the liver is a possibility as well. 
You are provided with a paperwork so you can have your liver 
function checked on ___. If liver enzymes 
remain concerning, liver biopsy will be needed to rule out graft 
versus host disease. Liver team has evaluated you during your 
stay and recommended that you follow up with them in the clinic. 


We made the following changes in your medication list:
- Please STOP bactrim because your liver enzymes are elevated
- Please STOP allopurinol
- Please TAKE compazine 10 mg every 6 hour as needed for 
nausea/vomiting if recur
- Please TAKE Lomotil every 6 hour as needed for loose stools if 
recur

Please continue the rest of your home medications the way you 
were taking them at home prior to admission.

Please follow with your appointments as illustrated below.

___ year old gentleman with Hx of AML, s/p cord transplant in

found to have norovirus infection.  He was also found to have 
transaminitis and acute renal failure on admission. Volume 
depletion and renal failure resolved, and GI symptoms gradually 
improved as well.  Transaminitis did not resolve and will be

positive.  While hospitalized, he was started on aggressive IV

his discharge he had no vomiting or diarrhea for > 24 hours.  He 
was discharged with a few tablets of compazine and lomotil in

decreased PO intake.  The patient was also initially found to be

patient's creatinine soon trended down back to his baseline.

avoided.  Upon discharge, the patient's creatinine had returned

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you've been feeling quite unwell with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea for about five days now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It started suddenly. I’ve barely been able to keep anything down. I’ve also been feeling dizzy, especially when I stand up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned some cramping in your lower abdomen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, crampy pain, nothing too severe, but constant. My stool started loose and got watery. No blood though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And you’ve noticed you’re urinating less than usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Definitely. I think that’s why I feel so weak and lightheaded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We checked your blood pressure lying down and standing — it drops when you stand, which confirms dehydration. We’re going to start you on IV fluids right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. I just want to feel more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, your labs came back. Your kidney function is impaired — creatinine is 3.0, which is high for you. Your baseline is around 1.8, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, usually around there. Is this serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning, but we believe it’s due to dehydration from the diarrhea and poor intake. Your FeNa is low, which supports that. With IV fluids, we expect it to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not permanent damage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this looks like acute kidney injury on top of your chronic kidney disease, and it should reverse as you rehydrate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed your liver enzymes are elevated — ALT is 360 and AST is 171. That’s something we need to monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My liver? I’ve had issues before with hemochromatosis. Could that be it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we’ve ruled out hepatitis viruses. The timing suggests it could be related to your current infection or possibly graft-versus-host disease. We’ll need to investigate further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool tests came back. It’s negative for C. diff, bacteria, and parasites. But it’s positive for norovirus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Norovirus? Like the stomach bug? I thought only kids get that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, adults get it too. It’s very contagious. You mentioned your wife had similar symptoms — that fits. It usually resolves on its own, but it hits harder in people like you with weakened immunity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s what’s causing all this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. We’ll keep supporting you with fluids until it passes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a flexible sigmoidoscopy tomorrow to check your colon. Even though norovirus explains your symptoms, we want to rule out graft-versus-host disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I’m feeling weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a short procedure, and we’ll use minimal sedation. It’s important to check for GVHD, especially with your liver enzymes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The sigmoidoscopy went well. We saw diverticulosis, but the biopsies didn’t show signs of GVHD. The pathologist noted only rare apoptotic cells, not enough to diagnose GVHD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very. And CMV testing was negative, so it’s not that either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So norovirus is the main culprit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. But we’re still concerned about your liver. The liver team thinks it could be norovirus affecting the liver directly, or a flare triggered by the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need a liver biopsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. You declined, and that’s okay. We’ll monitor your liver enzymes closely as an outpatient. If they don’t improve, we may revisit that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is down to 2.1 today — that’s a big improvement from 3.0. Your kidneys are responding well to fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. And my nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no vomiting in over 24 hours. We’re advancing your diet to soft foods today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m actually feeling hungry for the first time in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show creatinine is now 1.7 — back to your baseline. That’s excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: ALT and AST are still elevated — around 300. We’ll need to follow up closely. The liver team recommends outpatient monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do whatever’s needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping allopurinol. It’s not essential, and since your liver is inflamed, we want to reduce any potential burden.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that for years. Is it safe to stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially since your uric acid levels aren’t high. We can restart if needed later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also holding your Bactrim for now. It can affect the liver, and we don’t want to add risk while your enzymes are up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I need that for pneumonia prevention, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll restart it once your liver tests improve. Your oncologist will help coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no diarrhea for two days now. You’re walking well and eating without issues. We’re thinking you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home with some lomotil and compazine in case symptoms return. Take them only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your usual medications except allopurinol and Bactrim — those stay stopped for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: your creatinine is 1.6, and you’ve had no GI symptoms for over 24 hours. You’re stable for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need liver function tests three times this week. Your oncologist and liver clinic will contact you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my liver enzymes don’t improve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then we may discuss a liver biopsy. But for now, we’re optimistic they’ll trend down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re cleared to go home. You look much better — alert, walking, eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I really appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take the lomotil or compazine only if symptoms return, and call your doctor if they do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll get those liver tests done right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Stay hydrated, rest, and we’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — your HCV viral load came back negative. So hepatitis C isn’t contributing to your liver issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. That was on my mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All right, you’re all set. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I’ll follow up as instructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — you understand to restart Bactrim only when your liver tests normalize?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, not until my liver is better. Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And keep taking your prednisone and Cellcept — no changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Those are for my GVHD, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We didn’t change any of your immunosuppressants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time, including your medications and follow-up labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll listen carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check — any questions before you leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one last thing — my cough the other day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a chest X-ray — no pneumonia. The pulmonary edema from before has resolved. Your cough was likely mild and unrelated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Just wanted to make sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. All clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re officially discharged. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take it easy, and call if anything changes.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a 58-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia s/p allogeneic cord transplant and chronic graft-versus-host disease, was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea lasting five days. He was found to be dehydrated with orthostatic hypotension and acute kidney injury, with creatinine rising from a baseline of 1.8 to 3.0. IV hydration was initiated, and his renal function improved, returning to baseline by discharge. Stool testing was positive for norovirus, and flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsy showed no evidence of graft-versus-host disease. Liver enzymes remained elevated throughout admission, prompting consultation with the liver team and plans for close outpatient monitoring; allopurinol was discontinued, and Bactrim was held due to transaminitis. The patient's gastrointestinal symptoms resolved, and he was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up on liver function and restart medications as appropriate.
